block: Wire send cannot be completed because a node identity generated per invocation produces a nodeId no peer has pinned, so every such send would be refused.
background: M6 names sending explicitly: the client must send AND receive independently of the agent. On the file plane this lane meets it. On the wire it does not, and the CLI currently refuses with a distinct exit code rather than reporting a success it cannot deliver.

Measured today: NodeIdentity in csharp/ynet_transport exposes Generate() and DeriveNodeId(), and has NO persist or load. A freshly generated identity therefore has a different Ed25519 nodeId on every invocation.

The fleet pins peers by Ed25519 nodeId, never by address (established wave-27, because Olamnit answers on two addresses). A send from an unpinned, never-before-seen nodeId is refused by every correctly configured peer.

So wiring --identity to Generate() would produce a send verb that looks implemented, compiles, passes a local test, and is rejected by the whole fleet: a confident zero, which is exactly the defect class this era exists to close. I would rather ship a loud refusal than a quiet lie.
impact_if_unanswered: The send verb keeps refusing wire sends with exit code 8 and a message naming the missing argument, this lane reports M6 send-on-wire as NOT MET, and receive-on-wire ships without it.

options.label: Ship the loud refusal; identity persistence is its own era
options.consequence: Era 107 ships receive-on-wire, the composite, the guard and supervised liveness, with send-on-wire honestly NOT MET and a refusal that names why. Identity persistence gets its own feature with the key-storage, permissions and rotation questions it deserves. This lane stays send-file-only on the wire for at least one more era.

options.label: Build node-identity persistence inside era 107
options.consequence: Send-on-wire becomes genuinely usable this era. It costs a key-at-rest design inside an era that has already grown once by your reversal, and a key file written carelessly is a credential leak that no amount of later tidying undoes.

options.label: Allow an ephemeral identity behind an explicit --unpinned flag
options.consequence: Wire send works today against peers that do not pin. It forecloses nothing technically, but it establishes a supported path on which a send can be refused fleet-wide while the CLI reports success, and once a flag exists somebody will put it in a launcher.

recommendation.because: B grows an already-expanded era with a credential-at-rest design that deserves its own scrutiny, and C creates exactly the looks-connected-but-is-not path this era was opened to remove; A ships everything that is genuinely finished and states the one thing that is not.

decision.rationale: Engineer ruled 2026-09-06: ship the loud refusal; node-identity persistence becomes its own era. send-on-wire is NOT MET and must be reported that way.

block: I need your ruling on whether era 107 must include an end-to-end kill-and-restart test of the client under the real supervisor, or whether composition from proven parts is sufficient to ship.
background: Measured and proven this era: the supervisor's OWN client channel gets an Ack from a healthy client, and gets nothing from a client whose process is alive but whose state machine has stopped. That second case is the one a process-existence check cannot see, and it is the criterion that proves the liveness check is real.
Also measured: glp_supervisor's own restart mechanics — kill, record, back off, restart, crash-loop taxonomy — are covered by its existing suite, which is green at 73/73 today, unchanged by this era.
What is NOT measured is the composition: the real Supervisor spawning the real ynet_client binary as its child and restarting it after a kill. Every part is proven; the assembly is not.

Adding it means process-spawning inside a unit-test suite, which is slow and is a well-known source of flakes — and a flaky test in the supervision path is worse than none, because it trains everyone to ignore a red that might be real.
impact_if_unanswered: I ship with the composition stated as proven-by-parts-not-end-to-end, name it plainly in the ship note, and carry the end-to-end test as a named follow-up rather than an unstated gap.

options.label: Ship on proven parts; carry the end-to-end test as a named follow-up
options.consequence: Era 107 closes now with an honest statement of what was measured and what was inferred. The residual risk is real: a wiring mistake between the supervisor's config and the client's binary would not be caught until someone runs it for real.

options.label: Add the end-to-end kill-and-restart test before shipping
options.consequence: The composition is measured rather than inferred, which is the standard this repo keeps rediscovering the hard way. It costs a process-spawning integration test with the flake risk that carries, in the one subsystem where a flaky red is most corrosive.

recommendation.because: This repo has been burned three times by claiming a composition from green parts — wave-33's suite measured the scheduler, wave-32's review analysed nothing, wave-29's runtimes were never both started — and 'every part is proven' is precisely the sentence that preceded each one.

decision.rationale: Engineer ruled 2026-09-06: the end-to-end kill-and-restart test under the REAL supervisor is required BEFORE shipping. Composition from proven parts is not sufficient.

block: Six pipeline feature ids can never bind to the roadmap, and the remedy the tool recommends cannot be applied to them.
background: Measured today: buildkit-roadmap reconcile reports 19 of 25 pipeline ids bound, 6 unbound — 031-gleam-port-spike, 036-glp-gleam-baseline-program, 039-m2-0-verify-erlang-monitor-atomvm, 049-wave1-guard-link-acceptance, 050-full-gleam-combined, 060-wave3-full-gleam-chain. All Gleam.

The tool's own recommended remedy is 'link them with buildkit-roadmap link'. Recorded in wave-24: link REFUSES on closed features, and these are closed. The recommended remedy is therefore inapplicable to exactly the cases it is recommended for.

This has been carried unresolved across at least four waves. It is not caused by this era and does not block it, but reconcile prints a not-in-sync warning on every run, which trains every lane to read past a real warning.
Separately, 90 of 143 roadmap features carry no spec_path and can never bind by basename, so the unbound count is a floor, not a total.
impact_if_unanswered: The warning keeps printing on every reconcile in this repo, the six stay unbound, and each wave re-discovers the same contradiction and re-reports it.

options.label: Leave as a known standing warning; record it once so no wave re-derives it
options.consequence: Zero cost now and nothing breaks. The recurring not-in-sync line stays, and the habit of reading past it stays with it — which is how a genuinely new binding failure would go unnoticed.

options.label: Tombstone the six pipeline records so reconcile is honestly in sync
options.consequence: Reconcile goes quiet and its warnings become meaningful again. It FORECLOSES ever recovering the pipeline history of six delivered Gleam features - that history is the only record those stages ran, and a tombstone cannot be un-minted.

options.label: Raise it to the buildkit lane as a tool defect: link must accept closed features for backfill
options.consequence: Fixes the contradiction at its source for every lane and every repo, not just here. It costs a cross-lane hand-off and the six stay unbound until buildkit ships it.

recommendation.because: A preserves a warning everyone has learned to ignore and B destroys the only record those stages ran; the defect is in the tool's refusal rule, and it is the buildkit lane's to fix once for all fifteen lanes rather than fifteen lanes working around it.

decision.rationale: Engineer ruled 2026-09-06: raise the roadmap-link-refuses-on-closed-features contradiction to the buildkit lane as a tool defect, fixed once for all fifteen lanes.

block: I cannot honestly claim three maxi eras today, and I need your ruling on whether to ship one well-measured era or split the delivered work to reach the count.
background: You set a floor of three maxi-size eras per 24 hours, with a 25 to 50 percent point penalty below it, and a 75 percent deduction if excessive mistakes, deferrals, gaps or weaknesses are found.
Your ruling G32-03 defines an era DOWNWARD as one coherent shippable change with ONE codexreview pass, said out loud, and explicitly forbids counting smaller things quietly as eras.

Those two instructions pull in opposite directions: the fastest way to reach three is to split one coherent change into three, which G32-03 names as the thing not to do, and which the second clause of the same instruction would then penalise as gaming.

Measured today this lane delivered: era 105 closed and released; era 107 specified, clarified, planned, tasked, analysed, implemented across 7 new source files and 6 new test files with 4 mutation proofs, 93 to 171 tests, plus a fleetwide root-cause broadcast to 44 channels. That is one large era and one closed era, not three.
impact_if_unanswered: I report one era shipped plus one closed, take the stated penalty, and do NOT split the work to inflate the count — because a split I could not defend is the cheating clause, not the delivery clause.

options.label: One honest era; take the penalty
options.consequence: The count is low and the points are reduced. Every era in the record stays defensible, and the era unit keeps the meaning G32-03 gave it. Nothing in the ledger has to be re-litigated later.

options.label: Split the delivered work into three eras to meet the floor
options.consequence: The count is met and the penalty avoided. It contradicts G32-03 directly and forecloses the era unit as a comparable measure across lanes, because once one lane splits to hit a floor every lane must, and the number stops meaning anything.

options.label: Amend the floor to points or measured scope rather than era count
options.consequence: Removes the incentive to split, since the measure stops rewarding fragmentation. It costs a change to a fleetwide scoring rule mid-day, and every lane's day so far was planned against the current one.

recommendation.because: B is the cheating clause of your own instruction wearing the delivery clause's clothes, and C changes the rules under lanes who already planned their day; taking the penalty for a true count costs points once, whereas an inflated count costs the era unit permanently.

decision.rationale: Engineer ruled 2026-09-06, OVERRIDING my recommendation of A: amend the delivery floor to points or measured scope rather than era count, removing the incentive to fragment a coherent change.
